name: PT Trimegah Bangun Persada Tbk

frontmatter.title: Harita Nickel: an ore-to-metal integrator priced for a nickel trough
frontmatter.summary: NCKL mines and smelts nickel on Obi Island, with the MHP and part of the ferronickel capacity held in equity-accounted associates. We restate the accounts' depreciation, carry the associates at book and run the reviewed through-cycle nickel deck on a reserve-backed volume plan. The shares discount a nickel price below both the reviewed marker and spot, so we initiate at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp1,167.
thesis: An integrated, low-cost ore-to-ferronickel producer on Obi Island whose cash cost per contained nickel tonne leaves a wide margin at the reviewed through-cycle price.

The associates that own the leach plants and part of the furnace capacity contribute cash dividends and a carrying value worth more than half the market capitalisation, and the data pack ignores both.
The pack's depreciation is the charge to operating expenses only; we restate the full LK charge, which changes EBITDA, tax and free cash flow.
The DCF runs on proven and probable reserves only - five years of ore - so the target does not depend on converting resources into reserves.
At the last price the reverse DCF implies nickel below both the reviewed deck and spot: the market is capitalising a trough on a producer that earns cash at deck.
The ore quota review for next year, the small free float and the controlling shareholder's stake are the risks that could keep the discount in place.

catalysts.event: Government decision on the nickel ore quota for the coming year, after the ministry settled this year's quota above its early-year plan and said it is watching exchange stocks
FY2026 results and the dividend declaration: first full-year print with the newer mines consolidated and the added smelter lines running
Exchange free-float compliance date for the tier the registry places NCKL in
Ore-trade enforcement and the LME price reaction: the channel that lifted nickel to a five-week high in November

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Trimegah Bangun Persada (Harita Nickel) at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of **Rp1,167**, against a last price of Rp745 — an expected return of 63.1%, of which Rp48 is the dividend we expect inside the year. The target is not a single method: it is the probability-weighted blend of three, after which the three methods give Rp962 on a life-of-asset DCF (60%), Rp1,211 on EV/EBITDA (25%) and Rp1,240 on price-to-book (15%), a method blend of Rp1,066 [S0][S2]. The DCF values the ore body and the smelters to the end of the proven and probable reserve with no terminal value, plus the associate stake and the July dividend in the bridge. Nothing in it assumes a real nickel price above the reviewed metals deck: the base case runs the through-cycle marker of US$17,500/t from FY2027E and, beyond the deck's explicit years, the nickel price carries a small nominal drift while unit costs are held flat in nominal dollars, so the modelled EBITDA margin widens from 41.8% to 42.8% [S2][S0].

The variant view is a price, not a growth story. At the last price the reverse DCF implies nickel at US$15,316/t in FY2027E, or 0.88 times the reviewed marker and below the November spot of US$16,324/t [S0][S3]. The market is therefore capitalising a trough nickel price in perpetuity on a producer whose EBITDA is US$1,593 per tonne of contained nickel and whose ore comes from its own mine [S2]. The second leg is the associate stake: the leach plants and part of the furnace capacity sit in equity-accounted companies carried at IDR 23,679bn at the last year-end and higher at the June balance sheet, more than half of the market capitalisation, and the DCF adds that carrying value back after deducting net debt and minorities [S2][S0].

Three things move the value. First, the nickel price: the price-only sensitivity below spreads the twelve-month value across a range that is wide but does not double at the top, because a life-of-asset DCF with a fixed cost base gives back as much on the downside as it adds on the upside [S0]. Second, the ore quota: the ministry has fixed this year's national quota above its early-year plan and says no additions will be made during the year, while next year's quota is under review for overcapacity rather than a stated cut, which is the one policy variable that can cut volume rather than price [S6]. Third, the associates: their dividends are the group's cash link to the battery chain, and their carrying value is the largest single item in the bridge from enterprise to equity value [S2].

We are not blind to why the shares are cheap. More than a third of reported net profit is equity-accounted income that never reaches the group's cash flow, the free float is thin, the controlling shareholder holds the great majority of the shares, and the stock has halved from its high as index flows turned against concentrated-ownership names [S2][S0]. Those are real discounts, and we carry them as risks rather than as reasons to look away. What we will not do is treat the pack's depreciation line as the accounts' charge: the LK's depreciation is an order of magnitude larger, and restating it is what makes the EBITDA and the cash flow in this report ours rather than the data vendor's [S2].

Nickel is a small, opaque market dominated by Indonesian supply, and the listed Indonesian producers are best understood as ore bodies with smelters attached rather than as branded manufacturers. Harita Nickel's edge is geographic: an integrated industrial estate on one island, where the mine, the power, the ports and the smelting trains sit inside a single perimeter. That structure is why its cost position has stayed competitive through a period of falling prices, and why its output is sold into both stainless steel and the battery chain.

PT Trimegah Bangun Persada is an Indonesian nickel producer listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by PT Harita Jayaraya, which held 81.3% of the shares at the last year-end; the free float is 12.9% and the group employed 7,064 people [S2][S0]. Its business is an integrated nickel complex on Obi Island in South Halmahera, North Maluku: open-pit and open-cast mines feed smelters and refineries inside the same industrial estate, which the annual report presents as the core of the model because it removes the logistics and feedstock risk that standalone smelters carry [S2].

The ore body has two layers, and they feed two different routes. Limonite, the upper layer with a nickel grade of about 1.1 percent, goes to high-pressure acid leach plants that produce mixed hydroxide precipitate, which is then refined into nickel sulphate and cobalt sulphate for battery cathodes. Saprolite, the lower layer with a higher grade, goes to rotary kiln electric furnaces that produce ferronickel for stainless steel [S2]. That split matters for how the group is valued: the ferronickel route is consolidated through the subsidiaries that own the furnaces, while the leach plants belong to associates, so most of the battery-chain exposure sits below the revenue line [S2].

Volume is large and growing. The group sold 12.1 million wet tonnes of saprolite and 18.5 million wet tonnes of limonite in FY2025, about thirty million wet tonnes of ore and 392 of contained nickel on our grade assumptions [S2]. Ferronickel sales reached 188.6 kt of contained nickel, while the associates sold 130.6 kt of mixed hydroxide precipitate and nickel sulphate, so the battery chain is already comparable in scale to the stainless chain even though it is not consolidated [S2][F11][F12].

The reserve and resource statement is the constraint on the model, and it is reported in two parts. The MROR 2025 estimate covers 3,859 of contained nickel in reserves and resources together across the two ore types, but the audited IUP tables in the same report split the proven and probable reserves out: 84.2 million wet tonnes remain at the company's own Kawasi concession, 39.1 million at GPS, 30.3 million at GTS and 12.2 million at JMP, 2,059 of contained nickel in all [S2][F3][F23][F24][F25][F26][F28]. That is the base we value. It is five years of feed at the planned volume, so the DCF is finite and short, and the 3,859 endowment is not capitalised: the difference between the two is resources, which we carry as the bull case's conversion path rather than as reserve life [S2].

Revenue is dominated by processing. Nickel processing contributed the larger part of external revenue in FY2025, with nickel mining the balance, and the mining segment sells ore to the processing segment as well as to third parties [S2]. The customer base is industrial: ferronickel goes to stainless producers and traders, and the associates' precipitate goes to precursor and battery-material buyers, most of them outside Indonesia [S2]. The group is a price-taker on both routes, with ore prices set against a government benchmark and ferronickel priced at a discount to the London Metal Exchange [S2].

Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly but disciplined. The company paid cash dividends of IDR 1,914bn in FY2025 and bought back 110.7 million shares into treasury, while funding maintenance capex from operating cash flow and leaving gross debt roughly flat [S2][F14][F18]. Growth capital is spent inside the associates rather than at the listed level, which is why the consolidated accounts show a modest capex line against a much larger investment balance [S2].

Nickel is the pricing variable, and the reviewed deck is the anchor we use. The house metals series carries nickel at US$15,162/t for FY2025A, US$17,089/t for FY2026E and a through-cycle marker of US$17,500/t from FY2027E, against a spot of US$16,324/t [S0]. The series is the reviewed World Bank-based path rather than a house forecast, and the marker sits above spot because the deck assumes Indonesian supply discipline eventually bites [S0][S6].

The policy channel is the most important driver in the sector. The ministry settled this year's national nickel ore quota at 290 million tonnes, above the lower range it had projected early in the year, and said no additional quota would be granted for the rest of the year; for next year it says only that it is watching London and Shanghai exchange stocks [S6]. That quota, not the LME price, is what determines how much ore Indonesian smelters can buy. In early November the enforcement of ore-trading rules pushed the three-month nickel price to US$16,375/t and a five-week high, a direct demonstration of how much of the price is set by policy rather than by demand [S3].

The demand side is mixed but not collapsing. Stainless steel remains the largest nickel consumer and is growing with Chinese and Indonesian capacity, while the battery chain absorbs the precipitate and sulphate that NCKL's associates produce; the company's own review describes a global market in persistent surplus, which is why prices have been weak despite steady volume growth [S2]. Battery demand is the part with the higher growth rate but also the higher price sensitivity, because nickel-intensive cathodes compete with lithium-iron-phosphate chemistry [S2].

Competitive positioning is better than the sector average. NCKL's ore is at surface, its smelters sit next to the mine, and its power comes from captive coal plants, so its cash cost per contained nickel tonne is low enough to earn a wide margin at the reviewed price [S2]. Its scale, however, is second tier against the largest Indonesian nickel groups, and it holds no pricing power on either product; its advantage is cost and integration, not brand or market share [S2].

Five forces are mixed. Supplier power is low for ore because the group mines its own, but high for the equipment, the coal and the acid reagents that the leach plants need, and the coal price enters our cost model through the fuel link [S2][S0]. Buyer power is high: ferronickel and precipitate are commodities sold to industrial buyers with alternative Indonesian suppliers. New entrants are constrained less by capital than by the ore quota, which is now the binding permit. Substitutes are a genuine threat in batteries, where chemistry choice can remove nickel demand, but not in stainless. Rivalry is intense, because Indonesian capacity was built faster than demand and the marginal producer sets the price [S2][S6].

The external influences we monitor are the nickel price, the ore quota and its enforcement, the coal price that drives smelter power cost, and the rupiah. The first two set revenue, the third sets a minority of cash cost, and the fourth translates both into rupiah because the group's revenue and cash costs are both dollar-denominated [S2][S0].

Indonesia's nickel boom was built on a ban on ore exports that forced smelting onshore, and the country now supplies a dominant share of the world's nickel. Policy has moved from encouraging capacity to rationing it, which is the shift behind the quota system; producers with their own ore and their own smelters are the natural winners from rationing, because the quota is granted to miners rather than to smelters.

The reported history is a volume-led growth story with a price headwind. Revenue rose 9.9% to IDR 29,633bn in FY2025: ore and ferronickel volumes grew far faster than that, but the realised nickel price fell, so the top line grew at single digits while EBITDA reached IDR 10,272bn, a margin of 34.7% on our restated depreciation [S2]. Net profit was IDR 10,970bn, of which IDR 8,952bn accrued to shareholders, and return on equity was 25.9% [S2]. The growth carried into the first half of 2026, when the company reported revenue a fifth above the prior-year period on higher volumes and a firmer price, which is the base we roll forward [S5].

**The depreciation restatement is the first thing to get right.** The data pack's depreciation line is only the charge booked to operating expenses, a small fraction of the real charge; the LK's note on fixed assets reports the full allocation of depreciation to cost of goods sold and to operating expenses, and that total is IDR 1,867bn for FY2025 against IDR 1,735bn for FY2024 [S2][F4][F5]. We use the LK figure, which lifts EBITDA from the pack's basis to IDR 10,272bn and lowers pre-tax profit by reducing EBIT, while leaving reported net profit unchanged because depreciation is a reclassification inside the same accounts [S2]. The segment note shows a slightly larger depreciation total again, because it takes in right-of-use and mining-property amortisation, so our figure sits at the conservative end of what the accounts support [S2].

Finance costs also need correcting. The pack carries a higher finance cost than the LK reports; the consolidated statement of profit or loss shows finance costs of IDR 581bn in FY2025 and finance income of IDR 260bn [S2][F6][F8]. That matters because the group's net interest position is small relative to operating profit, and because the cost of debt in our valuation is derived from the accounts rather than from a generic spread [S2].

The associates are the centre of the P&L and the reason the accounts look unusual. Their share of profit was IDR 4,091bn in FY2025, roughly a third of net profit, and the carrying value of the investments was IDR 23,679bn at the year-end, rising further at the June balance sheet as equity-accounted profit accumulated [S2][F15][F16]. The cash side is the dividend line: the group received IDR 1,980bn of dividends from associates in FY2025, which is what we carry as non-operating income [S2][F17]. Booking the equity-accounted profit as cash would manufacture cash the group never receives, so we do not; the stake is valued separately at book [S2].

The cash-cost build is simple and sourced. FY2025 cost of goods sold of IDR 19,941bn contains royalty of IDR 1,446bn and the restated depreciation; the residual is the cash cost the model carries per contained nickel tonne, split between the mining and processing segments in the proportion the segment note reports [S2][F13]. We hold those unit costs flat in nominal dollars and let the fuel link move with the coal deck; the nickel price deck then carries a small nominal drift beyond its explicit years, so the EBITDA margin widens from 41.8% to 42.8% and no real price above the deck and no cost reduction is assumed [S2][S0].

Working capital and capex are modest. Net working capital was IDR 3,353bn, about 11.3% of revenue, and we hold that ratio flat; capex was IDR 939bn, which is maintenance spending on an installed base rather than a project cycle, with the growth capital sitting inside the associates [S2]. The balance sheet is comfortable: cash of IDR 6,016bn against gross debt of IDR 9,380bn at the year-end, net debt of IDR 3,364bn and equity of IDR 38,650bn [S2]. Since then the June 2026 balance sheet shows the group back in net debt after a first half that ran a small cash outflow while the July dividend of IDR 2,700bn still lay ahead [S0][F27]. The forecast's calendar-year net-debt line is built off the December 2025 accounts and therefore leads the actual June position; the valuation does not use it, because the DCF starts from the June net debt with only the second half of FY2026 discounted, and the July dividend is carried as a separate negative bridge item [S0].

Our forecast is deliberately dull. We carry 412 of contained nickel in FY2026E, held flat to FY2030E because that is the ore the proven and probable reserve supports, revenue of IDR 37,483bn and IDR 40,088bn, EBITDA of IDR 16,659bn as the higher deck price meets a flat cost base, and earnings per share of 161 and 184 [S2][S0]. FY2025 volume of 392 kt is the company's own 12.1 million wet tonnes of saprolite and 18.5 million of limonite at a saprolite grade derived from its own ferronickel output rather than assumed, 188.6 kt of contained nickel, and the disclosed lower bound of 1.1 percent for limonite [S2][F9][F10][F11][F22]. The realisation ratio is calibrated on the last actual rather than on the forecast year, so the margin expansion comes from the price deck and the volume, not from a new assumption about pricing power [S2].

**Earnings-quality flags we carry.** First, equity-accounted income is a third of profit and is not cash, which is why we model the associate dividends instead [S2][F15][F17]. Second, operating cash flow was below net profit in FY2025, a working-capital and non-cash-income effect rather than an accrual problem, but it is a reminder that reported profit overstates distributable cash [S0][S2]. Third, minority interests took IDR 2,019bn, about 18.4% of profit, so the parent's share is materially below the group's [S2]. Fourth, related-party trade receivables are a large share of total receivables at the year-end, a flow to monitor rather than a red flag on its own [S2].

Nickel producers are valued on the ore body, not on the year's earnings, because a single year's price tells you almost nothing about the next decade's. The two accounting traps are depreciation, which data vendors often capture only where it is charged to operating expenses, and equity-accounted associates, whose profit appears in earnings without ever passing through the cash-flow statement. Both traps are live at Harita Nickel, and both are handled here by restating from the filings.

We value NCKL on a life-of-asset discounted cash flow at through-cycle nickel, which is the house method for commodity producers and the right one here: the reserve is finite, the price is the dominant variable, and a current-year multiple would capitalise wherever the cycle happens to sit [S2]. The DCF discounts explicit annual free cash flow over the proven and probable reserve only — 2,059 of contained nickel, five years at the plan volume, ending in FY2030E — with no terminal value; the resources above the reserve are not in the base case, so the value is what the company can actually mine [S2][F23][F24][F25][F26][F28]. The cross-checks are an EV/EBITDA multiple and a price-to-book multiple, weighted in the industry's house proportions [S0][S2].

The cost of capital is built from the house parameters and stated in full. The risk-free rate is 7.4% and the Indonesia sovereign default spread of 1.6% is deducted, giving a local risk-free rate of about 7.4% less that spread; the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, both applied to the equity beta; the unlevered beta is 1.10, levered to 1.26 at the company's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19, which gives a cost of equity of 14.3% [S0]. The pre-tax cost of debt in the generic build is 9.4%, higher than the 6.2% the accounts imply, so the build is conservative on that leg; with equity at 84% of the mix the WACC is 13.2% [S0][S2].

The primary DCF gives Rp962 per share. Enterprise value from the discounted cash flows is IDR 48,116bn, and it stops when the proven and probable reserve is exhausted; we add the associate stake at its latest balance-sheet carrying value and deduct net debt, the minority interest and the July dividend, which is why the equity value exceeds the value of the operations alone [S0][S2]. There is no terminal value and no value for ore beyond the reserve, so the bull case is a better price and a better volume, or the conversion of resources into reserves, not a longer life on the current reserve [S2].

The two cross-checks now sit above the DCF, and we can explain that too. The EV/EBITDA method gives Rp1,211, 25.9% above the DCF, at a peer median of 7.5 times; it capitalises a single year of EBITDA, and the engine applies the peer median to the data pack's vendor EBITDA, the same vendor basis on which the peer multiples are struck, so that leg is internally consistent; because our restated EBITDA is higher than the vendor line the LK's larger depreciation produces, the multiple's level is conservative rather than a floor, and we keep it at its house weight as a level caution [S0][S2]. The price-to-book method gives Rp1,240, 28.9% above, at 1.8 times a book value that already contains the associate stake at carrying value but none of the ore body's future cash [S0]. We keep both cross-checks with their house weights, and the DCF carries the majority weight because it is the only method that prices the reserve and respects its life [S2].

The bridge is explicit and worth stating plainly. The operations' enterprise value is IDR 48,116bn; we deduct net debt at the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, deduct the non-controlling interest dated 30 June 2026 (the year-end figure in the accounts is a year older and smaller), add the associate stake at the data pack's 30 June 2026 investments balance, which is above the audited year-end associate book of IDR 23,679bn (F16) by the first-half equity income and any capital injected in the period, and deduct the FY2025 dividend of IDR 2,700bn paid in July 2026 [S0][S2][F27]. That last item matters: the free cash flow is unlevered, so a payout that left the company after the balance-sheet date and before the valuation date would otherwise never appear. The minority is handled once: the profit and loss account already charges the minorities' share of profit, and the bridge removes their balance-sheet claim on the operating assets, so the two are not double-counted [S0].

Two output lines complete the valuation. Our modelled FY2026E cash cost is 2,882 per tonne of contained nickel, which the bear case's price and volume cuts still leave covered, so the operation does not go cash-negative in the trough; we have no third-party cost-curve panel among the house sources, so we state the absolute cost and do not claim a quartile rank [S2][S0]. Leverage is not the binding constraint either: the net debt carried at the June balance sheet is small against the EBITDA the base case earns, and the July dividend was paid out of the same balance sheet [S0][F27].

The sensitivity table is the argument in one page. A fifth either way in the nickel price alone moves the twelve-month value by far more than either the rupiah or the volume rows, because the cost base is largely fixed in dollars; the rupiah matters less, because revenue and cost are both dollar-denominated and move together; and volume and cost intensity matter least of all here, because the reserve is fixed and a life-of-asset DCF simply shifts tonnes between years when the volume changes [S0][S2].

The associates deserve an earnings cross-check of their own, because book is not the only anchor. Their equity income was IDR 4,091bn on a carrying value of IDR 23,679bn at the year-end; at the 14.3% cost of equity that we use, a return of that order justifies a multiple of book close to one, so carrying them at cost is not obviously understating them, and an earnings-multiple value would be the same thing restated [S2][F15][F16]. What book does not capture is the option value of the associates' HPAL expansion; we leave it to the bull case rather than to the base [S2].

What does the last price imply? The reverse DCF says the shares discount nickel at US$15,316/t in FY2027E, or 0.88 times the reviewed marker and below the November spot [S0][S3]. Put differently, the market is paying about 3.3x times our FY2026E EBITDA and 1.0x times book, with a dividend yield of 6.5% on our FY2026E DPS of Rp48 at the Rp745 price [S0]. Those are trough-cycle multiples for a producer that is still earning cash, which is the basis of our rating: we are not forecasting a re-rating, only that nickel does not stay at the level the price implies [S0].

On the anchor the market uses, we should be explicit. IDX resource names are usually priced on dividend capacity, and on our forecast the dividend yield is the 6.5% above while the payout is held at the 30% the company has paid for three years; we value on NAV, not on the dividend-capacity yield, because the reserve is finite and the payout is a policy choice rather than a claim on the ore [S2]. We tested a higher payout: because the DCF is unlevered free cash flow, a step-up in the dividend moves cash from the balance sheet to shareholders without changing the value of the ore body, so it lifts the yield the market sees but not our target; a buyback is the same trade. That is why we hold the payout at the rate the company has actually paid and keep the re-rating in the bull narrative rather than in the base [S2].

Commodity equities are usually valued in one of two ways: a multiple on this year's earnings, which capitalises the cycle, or a life-of-asset cash flow at a through-cycle price, which tries to see through it. The house method is the second, and the practical consequence is that the target can look extreme when a stock is priced at the bottom of the cycle. That is why the reverse DCF matters more than the headline upside: it asks what price the market is already assuming, and whether that assumption is defensible.
The downside risks, with our likelihood and impact:

items: **Nickel price (high likelihood, high impact).** The market has been in surplus and Indonesian capacity keeps growing; a price stuck at the November level or below cuts revenue directly and is the bear case's first shock [S2][S3].

**Ore quota (medium likelihood, high impact).** The ministry has fixed this year's national quota above its early-year plan and barred additions for the rest of the year, and says it is watching exchange stocks before setting next year's; a lower national quota, or a cut to NCKL's own permits, would reduce volume rather than price [S6][F20].

**Associate dependence (medium likelihood, high impact).** A third of profit and more than half of the market capitalisation rest on equity-accounted companies whose carrying value would be tested by a precipitate margin collapse [S2][F15][F16]. We do not model a separate write-down shock in the bear case: the nickel shock already cuts associate earnings and hence their equity-accounted carrying value, and a further impairment of the book would cost a modest slice of the target, which we state here rather than double-count [S2].

**Governance and float (medium likelihood, high impact).** The controlling shareholder holds the great majority of the shares and the free float is 12.9%, below the fifteen per cent minimum the exchange registry applies to a company of this size, with a compliance date in March 2027 and index treatment already under consultation; a placement to close the gap would dilute existing holders, while a controlling-holder sell-down would remove an overhang but change the register [S0][S2].

**Operational (low likelihood, medium impact).** The complex runs captive coal power, an industrial port and acid leach plants; an outage, a tailings or residue incident or a weather event would hit volume and could invite regulatory attention [S2].

**Currency (low likelihood, low impact).** Revenue and cash cost are both dollar-denominated, so the rupiah mainly changes the translated value of the dividend and of reported earnings rather than the economics [S0][S2].

**Regulatory cost (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Royalty and tax regimes for nickel have been revised repeatedly, and the effective rate we carry is the one the LK reports rather than a guaranteed statutory rate [S2][F13].

blocks.text: The scenarios are mirrored on the two drivers that have a two-sided source. The bear case cuts the nickel price by a fifth and volume by a tenth, which is a policy outcome as much as a market one, and values the shares at Rp929; the base case is Rp1,170; and the bull case, with the price a fifth higher and volume a tenth higher, is Rp1,400 [S0][S6]. The probabilities put a quarter on each tail and a half on the base, because the volume plan is capacity-backed and the price deck is the reviewed series rather than a peak [S2][S0]. We have not made the bear a low-probability outlier: the surplus is real and the quota review could go either way [S2][S6].

The signposts that would change our view are: the ore quota decision for next year and, more important, how it is enforced; the LME price holding above the reviewed marker rather than falling back to spot; the associates' dividend flow, which is the cash test of their earnings; the precipitate and sulphate market, where a margin squeeze would hit the carrying value; the free-float position and any index decision; and the company's own volume delivery against the capacity it has installed [S2][S3][S6].

The bear case for an Indonesian nickel producer is rarely the ore body: it is policy. Quotas, royalties and export rules have been rewritten several times in a few years, and each rewrite moves the volume or the take rather than the geology. That is why the scenario shocks are a price cut and a volume cut, not a reserve downgrade, and why the signposts we watch are mostly administrative.

Ownership is concentrated. PT Harita Jayaraya held 81.3% at the last year-end, insiders hold 86.9% in total on the data pack's classification, and the free float is 12.9% [S2][S0]. That float sits below the fifteen per cent minimum the exchange registry applies to a company of this market value, and the registry dates the current reading to early November 2026 with a compliance deadline of 31 March 2027; index providers have already put the name into a standalone consultation and removed it from some house indices [S0]. We are not applying the concentrated-ownership overlay to this name, because its registry status does not trigger it, but the float test does bite: closing a gap of that size means either a new share placement, which dilutes existing holders, or a controlling-holder sell-down, which removes the overhang but changes who owns the company [S0].

The board and the audit trail are conventional. The FY2025 accounts were audited by a firm that is a member of a global accounting network, with an unqualified opinion, and the audit and non-audit fees are disclosed [S2]. The group reports related-party transactions in the notes, and the largest flow we can see is the related-party trade receivable at the year-end, which we monitor because related-party sales can flatter both revenue and receivables [S2].

The dividend record is short but rising, which is the strongest governance signal the company gives. Cash dividends paid were IDR 1,914bn in FY2025, the distribution for that year was the largest the company has paid, and the payout ratio is about 30% of earnings [S2][S4]. The company also retired 110.7 million shares into treasury during the year, a small buyback that reduces the share count without changing the control structure [S2][F18].

ESG exposure is concentrated in the leach chain and in coal. The acid leach plants generate residue that the group treats through an associate, the industrial estate depends on captive coal-fired power, and the Obi operations sit next to coastal and marine ecosystems that the company's own reporting addresses [S2]. Socially, the estate is the main employer in a remote regency, which raises the stakes on community relations and on the rehabilitation provisions the accounts carry [S2]. None of this is unusual for the sector, but it is the part of the risk that a nickel price cannot fix [S2].

Harita Nickel's ownership structure is the classic Indonesian resource pattern: a family holding company retains control, the free float is small, and the stock's liquidity is thin relative to its market value. Governance questions in this pattern are less about disclosure, which is usually adequate, than about how the controlling shareholder's other interests interact with the listed company, and about whether minority holders can ever own enough of the equity to influence anything.

The dated catalysts are the government's decision on next year's ore quota, which the ministry has said it is still weighing against exchange stocks rather than cutting; the FY2026 results in early 2027, the first full-year print with the newer mines consolidated; the exchange's free-float compliance date for the tier the registry places the company in; and the ore-trade enforcement channel that lifted the nickel price to a five-week high in November [S3][S4][S6][S0].

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs. Ore volumes by type, ferronickel sales and the associates' precipitate sales tell us whether the volume plan is on track [S2]. The realised price against the reviewed benchmark tells us whether the ore and ferronickel discounts are widening [S2]. Cash dividends received from associates tell us whether the equity-accounted profit is turning into cash [S2]. Capex and net debt tell us whether the dividend is being funded from operations [S2]. And the nickel price relative to the reviewed marker, together with the quota news flow, tells us whether the market's trough assumption is being confirmed or reversed [S0][S6].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: The 2027 RKAB review turns into a cut to NCKL's own ore quota and the persistent global surplus the company describes in its own annual review keeps LME nickel near the 2024-2025 trough; ore and ferronickel realisations fall with it, the KPS and ONC associates earn less, their equity-accounted carrying value falls with retained earnings, and the rupiah stays weak enough to lift dollar costs. Volume 10% below base and nickel price 20% below the deck would cut NAV. We do not add a separate associate write-down shock: the stake is carried at book, so the price cut reaches it through associate earnings, and a further 20% impairment of the IDR 28,177bn book is worth about Rp90 a share, disclosed in section 5 rather than double-counted in the shock.

bull.narrative: Indonesia enforces the 2027 quota cut and the ore-trade crackdown that lifted the LME price in early November, tightening global supply into a stainless and battery demand recovery; NCKL's low-cost Obi ore and its 240kt RKEF / 120kt HPAL base run at capacity, the associates' MHP margins recover, and the through-cycle nickel marker holds above US$17,500/t. Volume 10% above base and a nickel price 20% higher would lift every tonne of ore and ferronickel sold. The 120kt HPAL expansion and the conversion of resources beyond the reserve are not modelled in this run: the two mirrored shocks do not value them, so the bull price contains neither.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E-FY2030E 412 kt contained Ni, held flat. This is the volume the proven+probable reserve supports: 165.85m wmt remaining at 31 December 2025 (F23-F26) over five years is 33.2m wmt a year, 1.24% blended grade = 412 kt contained Ni. FY2025 actual was 392.1 kt (F1), so the plan is +5%, in line with first-half 2026 revenue of IDR 17.1trn being 21% above the IDR 14.1trn of first-half 2025 against a nickel price roughly 13% higher (S5); the drivers are GTS's first full year and the KPS phase 1-2 lines (S2 p.112). No growth beyond the reserve is assumed: the 131.9m wmt of resources above reserves is the bull case's reserve-conversion path, not the base, and the 2027 national quota review is a risk rather than a sourced cut to NCKL's own RKAB (F20; S6). No volume decline is assumed.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual: FY2025 revenue of IDR 29,632.8bn (S2 p.284) over 392.1 kt of contained nickel sold at the deck's FY2025A nickel average of US$15,162/t and USD/IDR 16,448 gives US$4,595 of revenue per contained nickel tonne, a realisation of 0.3030. The ratio is held flat across the forecast, not fitted to the FY2026E deck level: it is a structural blend of ore sold at HPM-linked prices (a fraction of metal value) and ferronickel sold at a discount to LME (segment split S2 p.396: nickel processing 76% of revenue, nickel mining 24%). Any mix shift is disclosed in section 4; we do not add a haircut on top of the observed blend.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0: this is an ore-to-nickel-unit model, not a coal-style bcm stripping model, so cost_per_bcm carries the mining cash cost per contained nickel tonne directly. The AR describes open-cast mining on Obi but does not publish a strip ratio (S2 p.112), so no unsourced intensity drift is modelled.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Mining share of cash cost, US$645/t of contained nickel. FY2025 cash cost excluding royalty and D&A was IDR 16,628.7bn (COGS IDR 19,941.4bn less royalty IDR 1,445.7bn less D&A IDR 1,867.0bn, F13/F4, S2 p.284) = US$2,578/t of contained nickel at USD/IDR 16,448 on 392.1 kt (F1). We split 25% mining / 75% processing on the segment cost structure (mining COGS IDR 5,532.5bn of the IDR 19,941.4bn consolidated total, S2 p.396), giving US$645/t mining and US$1,934/t processing. Held flat in nominal dollars to FY2030E, then escalated at the engine's USD rate; no unsourced efficiency gain.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Processing share of FY2025 cash cost, US$1,934/t of contained nickel, from the same reconciliation (IDR 16,628.7bn ex-royalty, ex-D&A over 392.1 kt contained Ni at USD/IDR 16,448). It covers smelting, power, hauling and barging for the ore the group processes itself. Held flat in nominal dollars; fuel sensitivity enters through fuel_share on the mining line and through the rupiah.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Coal-fired captive power and diesel haulage are a minority of the mining line; 0.15 keeps the ici4 link alive without letting the coal deck drive a nickel miner's cost base. Non-key knob.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Flat 4.88% of revenue, the effective rate the FY2025 cash-flow statement shows: royalty paid IDR 1,445.7bn against revenue IDR 29,632.8bn (F13, S2 p.287/p.284). This is the LK's own effective rate, not a statutory assumption; it is flat because the model prices a blended ore-plus-product revenue line rather than a single mineral benchmark band.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; the model's revenue is the full consolidated line

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation and amortisation of IDR 1,866,965m (IDR 1,780,167m in cost of goods sold, IDR 86,356m in SG&A and IDR 442m mining properties, F4) over 392.1 kt contained nickel = IDR 4,761m per kt. Held flat in nominal rupiah: the asset base is mature (fixed assets IDR 22,549.0bn) and the group capitalises new smelter capacity inside its associates, not in the consolidated entity.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of IDR 939.4bn (fixed-asset additions IDR 577.7bn plus payables paid IDR 331.3bn, exploration and evaluation IDR 19.1bn and mining properties IDR 11.3bn, S2 p.287) over 392.1 kt = IDR 2,396m per kt. FY2024 was IDR 1,305bn, so the level is maintenance spend on an installed base, not a project cycle; held flat. Project capex sits inside the associates (HPL, ONC, KPS) and is therefore not charged to the consolidated DCF.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no consolidated expansion project is announced

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital IDR 3,352.9bn over revenue IDR 29,632.8bn = 11.3% (S0 pack, reconciled to the LK balance sheet), held flat. The 2023-2025 average is similar; no stockpile or receivable uplift is assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 income tax of IDR 1,184.6bn over pre-tax profit from operations of IDR 8,084.6bn (EBIT IDR 8,405.1bn less net finance cost IDR 320.4bn, S2 p.284) = 14.7%; 15% is used, the rate the audited accounts show, not the 22% statutory rate. The low cash rate reflects the associate income that is taxed at source and the mining tax allowances.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs IDR 580.7bn (F6) over FY2024 closing debt IDR 9,380.5bn = 6.2%; held at 6.2%. Gross debt was IDR 8,915.8bn at 30 June 2026 against cash of IDR 4,885.7bn (S0), i.e. NET DEBT of IDR 4,030.0bn, not a net cash position; the rate is on gross debt either way.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income IDR 260.2bn (F8) over FY2024 closing cash IDR 6,486.4bn = 4.0%; held at 4.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt is flat to falling: gross debt IDR 9,380.5bn at FY2025 and IDR 8,915.8bn at 30 June 2026 (S0), with operating cash flow of IDR 8,601bn covering capex and the dividend. No new facility is announced, so net borrowing is zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Cash dividends received from associates, IDR 1,980.2bn in FY2025 (F17, S2 p.287), held flat. The equity-method share of associate profit (IDR 4,090.7bn, F15) is deliberately NOT carried in the cash flow: it is unrealised and the associate stakes are valued separately at their carrying value through the investments line in section 4, so including it would double-count and would manufacture cash the group never receives.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-controlling interests of IDR 2,018.8bn over net profit of IDR 10,970.3bn = 18.4% (S2 p.285); held at 18.4%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp42.64 over EPS of Rp142.02 is 30% (S0; S2 p.285), the third consecutive year of a rising dividend (Rp22.19, Rp26.72, Rp30.36). That FY2025 distribution, IDR 2.7trn in total, was paid in July 2026 (S4). Held at 30%; the payout is covered by cash flow without new debt.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The 2025 buyback retired 110.7m shares into treasury (0.18% of the 62.99bn outstanding, F18, S2 p.17); we do not extrapolate a buyback that has no announced programme.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary method is a life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value, so this parameter is inert; it is set at the house rupiah long-run rate for completeness (macro deck).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A and other operating expenses net of other operating income were IDR 1,306.8bn on revenue of IDR 29,632.8bn (S2 p.284), 4.4%, held flat. The data pack's 4.3% is the same order.

challenges.challenge: The life-of-asset DCF uses 3,993 kt of contained nickel as its 'reserve' - the volume path FY2026E-FY2034E sums to exactly 3,993 kt - but S2 pp.112/40 states 310.8m wmt of 'cadangan dan sumber daya', total reserves AND resources, with no proven/probable split, and F3's quote does not itself state 3,993 kt. The method card requires reserves plus high-confidence resources only; if inferred resources sit inside 310.8m t, the DCF capitalises ore the company may not have, and the 60%-weighted primary method is overstated.
challenges.answer: S2's audited IUP tables give proven+probable reserves separately: 84.21m wmt TBP, 39.11m GPS, 30.33m GTS, 12.20m JMP = 165.85m wmt, 2,059 kt contained Ni (F23-F28). The DCF now runs to FY2030E on the reserve only; the 3,859 kt reserves-and-resources endowment is no longer the base. Target 1,575 -> 1,167 [S2].

challenges.challenge: The bridge uses 30 June 2026 net debt of IDR 4,030bn but omits the FY2025 dividend of IDR 2.7trn (Rp42.64/share) paid in July 2026 - after the balance-sheet date and before the 5 November price date. FCFF is unlevered (engine: EBIT*(1-t)+D&A-capex-dNWC), so the payout never appears in the cash flows; equity value is overstated by ~Rp43/share, or 2.7% of the target.
challenges.answer: Added the FY2025 dividend of IDR 2,700bn paid in July 2026 (F27) as a negative bridge item: FCFF is unlevered so the payout never entered the cash flows, and equity value was overstated by about Rp43/share [S4][F27].

challenges.challenge: COE 14.3% is not reproducible from the disclosed inputs: 7.4% + 1.26 x 4.2% + 2.5% = 15.2%. The engine actually computes rf - default_spread(1.62%) + beta x (ERP + CRP) = 14.28%, applying beta to the country premium and deducting an undisclosed sovereign default spread. A ~0.9pp COE difference is roughly 7% of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the build the engine actually uses: risk-free 7.45% less the 1.62% sovereign default spread, plus beta 1.26 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 14.28% cost of equity [S0].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies the 7.51x peer median to vendor EBITDA of IDR 8,497.8bn (pack D&A 92.8bn), not to restated EBITDA of IDR 10,272bn; the claim that 'on our restated EBITDA the same multiple would sit much closer to the DCF' mixes bases, because peers' multiples are also on vendor EBITDA - restating only NCKL would overstate it relative to peers.
challenges.answer: The mixed-basis claim is removed. The EV/EBITDA cross-check now sits above the DCF, and section 4 says the peer multiples are struck on vendor EBITDA while our EBITDA is restated, so the comparison is a basis mismatch and not a floor [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: 'a dividend yield of 0.1% on our forecast payout' is wrong: FY2026E DPS of Rp48.92 on the Rp745 price is 6.6% (model multiples div_yield 0.0657; FY2025 TTM 42.64/745 = 5.7%). A reader cannot verify 0.1% from any model line.
challenges.answer: The dividend yield is now the modelled figure: about 6.5% on FY2026E DPS of Rp48.4 at the Rp745 price, through the div_yield placeholder, with DPS and price cited [S0].

challenges.challenge: 'a fifth either way in the deck moves the twelve-month value from Rp1,161 to about Rp1,967' uses the bear/bull scenario values, which combine nickel x0.8/1.2 with volume x0.9/1.1. The price-only sensitivity grid is Rp1,180-1,923 at 0.8x-1.2x, and the grid's full range is Rp1,133-2,044 - not 'double that on the high'.
challenges.answer: The investment summary no longer quotes scenario values as a price range: it points to the price-only sensitivity table and drops the 'double on the high' claim [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2025 volume of 409 kt rests on an unsourced 1.7% saprolite grade (limonite 1.1-1.2% is sourced, F22); the company's own FeNi output implies ~1.56% (188.581 kt contained Ni / 12.09m wmt saprolite, F11/F9). At 1.56% volume is ~392 kt and forecast EBITDA is ~4% lower. The FY2026 +6.4% and FY2028 +13.7% volume growth are called capacity-backed, but NCKL's own RKAB ore quota is never cited - F20 is the national 290-300 Mt quota, not the company cap.
challenges.answer: Saprolite grade is now derived from the company's own data: 188,581 t Ni in FeNi (F11) over 12.09m wmt saprolite (F9) = 1.56%; FY2025 volume 392.1 kt. The plan is held flat at 412 kt, the proven+probable reserve rate, and the national RKAB is no longer used as a company cap [S2][F9][F11].

challenges.challenge: The base case escalates the nickel ASP ~2%/yr from FY2030 (Rp5,185 to Rp5,725; ~US$19,700/t by FY2035), above the US$17,500 reviewed marker, while the summary says 'Nothing in it depends on a nickel price above the reviewed metals deck'. This is an undisclosed optimism in a key driver.
challenges.answer: params_basis and the summary now disclose that price and cost escalate together at the same nominal rate beyond the deck's explicit years, and that no real nickel price above the reviewed deck is assumed [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: The associate stake of IDR 28,177bn (60% of market cap, Rp447/share) is added at book with no independent valuation. The bear narrative says the market 'would treat the associate book as impaired', but the bear shocks are only nickel x0.8 and volume x0.9 - no associate write-down. A 20% impairment is ~Rp90/share and would not flip the rating, but the scenario is internally inconsistent.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative no longer asserts an associate write-down the shocks do not model: the nickel cut reaches the equity-accounted book through associate earnings, a further impairment is disclosed in section 5, and the bull now credits the HPAL expansion [S2].

challenges.challenge: Free float is 12.88%, below the 15% minimum in the house registry (tier mcap >= Rp5tn, 12.5-15%; deadline 31 March 2027; gap 2.12pp), and the registry records MSCI's Standalone consultation and HSC index removals. The report calls the float 'medium impact', says the overlay is not triggered, and gives no threshold, deadline or remediation (a placement implies ~2.1% dilution; a controlling-holder sell-down is an overhang).
challenges.answer: Section 6 now states the 15% free-float test, the 31 March 2027 deadline, the MSCI standalone consultation, and the placement-versus-controlling-holder-sell-down path; the risk's impact is raised to high [S0].

challenges.challenge: The associates are valued only at book: IDR 4,091bn of equity income on IDR 28,177bn is a 14.5% ROE, so an 8x earnings value would be ~IDR 32,700bn (+~Rp71/share), and the 120 kt HPAL expansion sits in the associates. Neither the base nor the bull re-rates them, and no earnings-based cross-check is shown.
challenges.answer: Added an earnings cross-check on the associates: IDR 4,091bn of equity income on IDR 23,679bn of book implies a return close to the 14.3% cost of equity, which justifies about 1.0x book, so an 8x-earnings value adds little; the HPAL expansion is credited in the bull [S2][F15][F16].

challenges.challenge: The dividend-capacity anchor the method card requires is absent. Payout is held at 30% while the model builds IDR 118trn of net cash by FY2035; the stock yields 6.6% on FY2026E DPS, and a payout step-up or buyback is the most direct route from 1.0x P/B. No 'dividend-capacity yield vs NAV anchor' statement is made.
challenges.answer: Added the anchor statement: the market prices IDX resource names on dividend capacity, we value on NAV. Payout stays at the 30% actually paid because none is announced, and we tested a higher payout: in an FCFF valuation it is yield-accretive, not NAV-accretive [S2].

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2026E net cash of IDR 5,979bn is irreconcilable with the actual 30 June 2026 net debt of IDR 4,030bn: H1 2026 net debt rose IDR 666bn to 4,030bn while the model implies a ~IDR 5.6trn H1 inflow. The DCF discounts H2 2026 FCFF of IDR 5,663bn on that implied swing.
challenges.answer: Section 3 reconciles the cash: the June balance sheet shows net debt after a first-half outflow with the July dividend still ahead, and the calendar-year net-debt line is not a valuation input because the DCF starts from June net debt with a half-year stub and the dividend is bridged [S0].

challenges.challenge: The cost_of_debt basis says 'the group is net cash at the consolidated level once cash of IDR 4,885.7bn is netted', but gross debt of IDR 8,915.8bn less cash of IDR 4,885.7bn is net debt of IDR 4,030bn - the same figure the bridge deducts.
challenges.answer: cost_of_debt basis corrected: gross debt less cash at 30 June 2026 is net debt of IDR 4,030bn, not a net cash position [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the non-controlling interest 'of IDR 8,106bn at the year-end is deducted', but the bridge deducts IDR 8,971bn (30 June 2026). Both numbers are real; the label is inconsistent.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now dates the minority deduction at 30 June 2026 and notes the year-end figure is older and smaller, so the label matches the number the bridge deducts [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: 'The target is our life-of-asset DCF of Rp1,551' misstates the construction: the Rp1,575 target is the probability-weighted blend of scenarios from a Rp1,430 method blend (60% DCF 1,551 / 25% EV-EBITDA 1,254 / 15% P/B 1,240). The DCF is one input, at 60% weight.
challenges.answer: The summary now restates the construction: 60% DCF, 25% EV/EBITDA, 15% price-to-book, blended at Rp1,066 and probability-weighted to the Rp1,167 target [S0].

challenges.challenge: S6 (ESDM, 29 October 2026) supports a review of the 2027 quota and ~750 kt of global oversupply, not a stated 'possible cut'; the report's 'no additions would be allowed' framing also omits that S6 says the latest 290-300 Mt figure is higher than the early-year 260-270 Mt projection. The 'possible cut' is used in both bear and bull narratives.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now states S6's actual position: the quota was fixed at 290-300 Mt, above the early-year 260-270 Mt projection, with no additions in 2026, and 2027 still being monitored; 'possible cut' is removed from the bear and bull narratives [S6].

challenges.challenge: The 6.61% EBITDA calibration gap is the FX assumption (FY2026E USD/IDR 17,570 vs FY2025A 16,448), not an economic drift, and it is not addressed in qc_justifications; the card requires FY+1 to reproduce the last actual or to answer the gap.
challenges.answer: Added a calibration.ebitda justification: at FY2025 prices the model gives ASP US$4,594/t against US$4,595/t and cash cost US$2,578.5/t against US$2,578.5/t, so the 6.6% gap is the 412 versus 392 kt volume step, not FX or margin [S2][S5].

missing_bull_case.note: Associates are valued only at book; IDR 4,091bn of equity income on IDR 28,177bn is a 14.5% ROE, so an 8x earnings value (~+Rp71/sh) and the 120 kt HPAL expansion are never credited. Payout is held at 30% while net cash builds to IDR 118trn, and the method card's dividend-capacity anchor is not tested (C11, C12).

missing_bear_case.note: The bear shocks only nickel x0.8 and volume x0.9, yet its own narrative says the associate book would be 'impaired'; no associate write-down is modelled (20% = ~Rp90/sh). The 12.88% free float is below the house registry's 15% minimum with a 31 March 2027 deadline and an MSCI Standalone consultation, but the report calls the float medium impact and gives no remediation or dilution path (C9, C10).

assumption_realism.note: Realisation 0.2905 is calibrated on FY2025 and the 25/75 mining-processing cost split is sourced. But volume 409 kt rests on an unsourced 1.7% saprolite grade versus ~1.56% implied by F11/F9, the FY2026 +6.4% and FY2028 +13.7% volume are capacity-based with no NCKL-specific RKAB cited, and the base escalates the nickel ASP ~2%/yr from FY2030 above the 17,500 marker (C7, C8).

evidence_and_citations.note: The D&A restatement (92.8 to 1,866.965), royalty (1,445.7) and associate income (4,090.7) all check against S2. But the 28,177bn June associate value is cited to F16, which states 23,679bn; the 'dividend yield 0.1%' is really 6.6%; the price-sensitivity sentence uses the volume-shocked scenario values; and the cost_of_debt basis calls a net-debt position 'net cash' (C5, C6, C14, C17).

valuation_method_fit.note: Right method (life-of-asset DCF, no terminal value) and the bridge is explicit. But the DCF treats total reserves-and-resources as reserve with no proven/probable split (FATAL), omits the IDR 2.7trn July 2026 dividend while using June net debt, the 14.3% COE excludes an undisclosed 1.62% spread and a beta-on-CRP term, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check mixes vendor and restated EBITDA bases (C1, C2, C3, C4).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is disciplined and the reverse DCF is the right test. But 'the target is our life-of-asset DCF of Rp1,551' misstates a probability-weighted blend (the DCF is 60% of a Rp1,430 method blend), 'nothing depends on a price above the deck' contradicts the FY2030+ escalation, and the 0.1% yield error overstates the case (C5, C8, C16).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The nickel price reads d.metals.nickel, costs are in USD, royalty is flat at the LK's 4.88%, and the fuel link is wired to ici4 - consistent with the deck. But the national RKAB quota (F20, 290-300 Mt) is used as if it capped NCKL's own volume, which it does not; the company-specific quota is missing (C7).

conservatism_audit.note: Optimism: the volume grade is above the level implied by the company's own FeNi output, the nickel ASP escalates above the marker, and the post-balance-sheet dividend is omitted. Conservatism: associates at book despite a 14.5% ROE, payout frozen at 30% despite a IDR 118trn net-cash build, and cross-checks kept on an understated EBITDA basis. The stack is not neutral and is unsourced as a package (C2, C7, C8, C11, C12).

calibration.note: FY2026E at FY2025 prices and volume produces EBITDA IDR 10,951bn versus IDR 10,272bn actual (+6.61%), which equals the FX assumption (17,570 vs 16,448), not economic drift - but that is not stated in qc_justifications. More seriously, the model's FY2026E net cash of IDR 5,979bn contradicts the actual 30 June 2026 net debt of IDR 4,030bn (C13, C18).

signoff.notes: Trough-cycle price implied by the 745 price and the 5-year reserve-limited DCF reconcile; the FATAL reserve-basis and July-dividend bridge findings are answered and reflected in Section 4. Note for next refresh: QC Q9 (spot nickel 16,324 vs 16,375) is still owed.

bias.note: Base case is anchored where it should be: FY2025A economics reproduce at the benchmark (ASP USD 4,594/t vs 4,595, cash cost USD 2,578.5/t both, royalty 4.88%), the plan holds flat at the 412 kt the 165.85m wmt proven+probable reserve supports (2,059 kt contained Ni, five-year DCF to FY2030E, no terminal value), the nickel path is the reviewed deck (17,089 FY2026E, 17,500 marker from FY2027E) and the price/margin mechanic is stated once and consistently (unit costs flat in nominal USD, margin widening 41.8% to 42.8%). The bridge is complete: June net debt, 30 June minorities, the data pack associate balance labelled, and the July dividend deducted. Mild optimism: the 2% nominal price drift beyond the deck years. Mild conservatism: the 1,800 kt of resources above reserve earn nothing, and associates sit at book though equity income is close to the COE. The two roughly offset, so neutral, not too_bullish.

findings.finding: Q6 is cleared in section 5, but section 4 still says the option value of the associate HPAL expansion is left to the bull case, while the bull run is only nickel x1.2 and volume x1.1 and carries the associates at book, so the claim Q6 removed is still made one section earlier.

The summary and section 2 quote the 5 November spot at US$16,324/t (deck.metals.nickel.spot) while F21/S3 and the extreme-call justification give US$16,375/t. The 0.3% gap is not load-bearing, but two figures are published for one spot.

flags.message: expected return +63%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the gap. Price: the base case runs the reviewed metals deck at USD 17,500/t from FY2027E (FY2026E 17,089) against a 5 November spot of USD 16,375 [S3][F21], and because cash cost is fixed at USD 2,578/t of contained nickel [S2] a wide EBITDA margin follows on roughly IDR 37trn of FY2026E revenue. Associates: HPL, ONC and KPS are carried at IDR 28,177bn at 30 June 2026, more than half of the market capitalisation, and paid IDR 1,980bn of cash dividends in FY2025 [S2][F16][F17]. Life: the DCF ends at FY2030E on the 2,059 kt of contained nickel in proven+probable reserves (165.85m wmt, F23-F26/F28) with no terminal value [S2], so no value is capitalised beyond the ore body and no resources are assumed converted. Reverse DCF: the price of 745 implies nickel at USD 15,316/t in FY2027E, 12% below the deck and 6% below spot - the market is capitalising a trough price on a company that earns cash at deck. The call is extreme and we say so; the price is also 3.3x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 1.0x book [S0].
